title: Hit by a car at ten and hiding the injury out of fear
summary: Cobb traces the bone condition to being struck by a streetcar-area car as a boy, running off so his mother wouldn't learn, and suffering for years.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: And I knew when I got it -- I got it when I was 10 years old. I got hit by a car.

Downtown here in Houston, Texas. My aunt worked at the theatre, and I could go there and go in for free. During that time, your trolley car, or streetcar, or whatever you want to call it was full-service for a student, and I'd take my lunch money and go down my mother's at work, and she didn't know I was at the movies, but my aunt let me in.

So I went down and come out between shows, and go across the street and get me a sandwich at the Greek restaurant, and I'm in a hurry to get back to the movie to catch what I wanted to catch, and I ran a light, and as small as I was, I couldn't see, I ran ... and the man hit me. Pow. Fell out in the street. Everybody crowded around -- here's a a little kid laying

in the street; somebody said, "Call an ambulance" -- they should have never said it. I jumped up and ran -- I didn't want my mother to know about it. [You know]how kids think. I didn't know I was hurt. I went back in the theatre and sat down; got away from these people talking about calling an ambulance -- if they called an ambulance, my mother would have gotten a report of it.
And I snuk away from home ... I sneaked away. She didn't know I was there. I would get up in the morning, and couldn't hardly -- it was like I had rheumatism or something, and as young as I was.
In the back. See, that's where all my trouble was, in the back, and I couldn't hardly straighten up. But once I straightened up and got the circulation going, I was all right.

And finally, my aunt called me one morning and she said, "Boy, you act like an old man." I said I was keeping this in my own (unintelligible) and I ain't telling nobody. This went on for years. I would go out -- after I bought a car and put it in the garage, and raised the garage door up, and it would kill me in my back. I mean it could be hot out, but anything that I would grab and pick up, or pick up, but as long as I didn't grab the thing but one time, just once, and once I got up, it was all right. And this thing went on and on.

And you know when I told my mother? I was married and had gone to New York; she had moved from Houston to New York afterwards, and then I told her. And she wanted to go down my throat and wanted to know why I didn't tell her ... but I had suffered. Suffered because I had fear. See, I had come up with fear, because kids were threatened in those days; "If you do this" or "If you do that" -- and that's why it's not good to cast fear in kids today. Because they don't have no confidence or trust and they scared something's gonna happen to them.

And love is the greatest force in the world. But my mother loved me. My grandfather loved me; he loved his kids. But I said they had a poor way of showing it, when they cast fear in you. Am I saying the wrong thing?
